title: Blues and Pentatonics
goal: Solo over a twelve-bar blues in A, knowing where the changes are and landing on notes that belong to them.
assumes: You know the open chords and can fret and pick single notes, and you can play eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM. Nothing about scales or blues is assumed. New ideas arrive in A, on purpose, so that theory is the only new thing, and the Steps after them move to other keys. This is a long Path: about three months at fifteen to twenty minutes a day.

skills: Eighth notes with a click at 70 BPM

orderRationale: Theory arrives as written lines you can be graded on, and choosing your own notes comes after, as a short 'your turn' at the end of a Step. Chord tones arrive early, as soon as the box is in the hand, as arpeggios of A7, D7 and E7 in box 1, each followed by a lick that ends on the chord's third, before the blue notes: knowing where the chord is matters more than knowing an extra note. Call and response follows because written answers to one call teach phrase length and endings with almost no theory. The blues scale and bends come after the player can find the chord tones, so neither becomes a thing to sit on. A second box comes late on purpose: more notes before good choices makes for faster bad solos. Guide tones come near the end because they are the most abstract idea here and easiest once the form is in the ear. Slow blues comes last as it hides nothing. Between the ideas sit Steps that add little or nothing new: the box in other keys, the same notes over a straight band, the thirds in new keys, the quick change, the minor blues, two more boxes, and sixths. The blues is a style a player stays in for months, and each of those Steps takes what was just learned somewhere new before the next idea arrives.
gradingLimits: Graded Exercises are written lines: the app checks timing evenness, notes heard and extra notes, and right notes after the take where the notes are single, far enough apart and not ringing into each other; elsewhere right notes read 'not checked'. Timing over the shuffle band is judged against the written triplet with a looser bar, so a lighter or heavier swing is not marked down, and a constant lean behind the beat costs nothing at all. The right-note check has only been tried on computer-made guitar sound with no band in the mix, so direct input or headphones are the honest way to play anything with a band; with a microphone and speakers it is untested. A bent note would read as a wrong one, so bends are timed and never pitch-checked: the unison bends are double stops, which the note check leaves alone. Landing on chord tones, staying in the scale, keeping rests and choosing your own notes are not measured today: those Exercises are 'your turn', self-checked and labelled 'not checked yet'. Nothing here grades feel.

steps.title: Pentatonic box 1
steps.goal: Play the A minor pentatonic box over a shuffle band, find its three A's inside a riff, and play your first twelve bars.
steps.why: These five notes are most of the blues and rock you've ever heard. Learning one box well, and knowing which note is the root, gets you playing over a band today. Without the roots, the box is a pattern: with them, it's a map you can navigate. Everything here is played with the band from the first note, because the box only makes sense against a groove.
howTo: First finger stays on fret 5, one finger per fret. The notes are A, C, D, E, G, and every string uses two of them.
The three A's are home: fret 5 on the low E, fret 7 on the D string, fret 5 on the high E. Every Exercise in this Step starts or lands on one of them, so say 'A' when you get there.
Shuffle eighths are long-short, on the band's triplet: say 'tri-pl-et' and play on the 'tri' and the 'et'. Damp strings you aren't using with the side of your picking hand.
steps.payoff: You can play a whole twelve-bar chorus over a shuffle band, and you always know where home is.

exercises.title: Box 1 over the shuffle
exercises.purpose: Put the shape in the hand with the band behind you: up the box, the top A held, back down, and home on the low A. Four bars that loop, so the scale turns into a groove.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1 climbs from the low A at fret 5 to D on the G string. Bar 2: E, G, A, C on the top two strings, then hold the high A for two beats. Bar 3 comes down to the A on the D string, a quarter note on beat 3, then G. Bar 4: E, D, C and the low A, held.
First finger on fret 5, third finger on fret 7, fourth on fret 8. Say the A's out loud as you pass them.
exercises.coachLine: Right notes and the shuffle are what this asks. Tempo isn't the point yet.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Find the three A's
exercises.purpose: The root is home, and every phrase you make will be judged by your ear against it. Here one little riff starts from each A in turn, low, middle and high, so you find them without looking, in time, with the band.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Four bars that loop.

Bar 1 from the low A (low E string, fret 5): A, C, D, C, A, C, D, E. Bar 2 from the middle A (D string, fret 7): A, C, D, C, A, G, E, G. Bar 3 from the high A (high E, fret 5): A, C, A, G, E, G, A, G. Bar 4: E, D, C, D, and the middle A held for two beats.
Every bar starts on an A. Listen to the same note in three octaves, and to how the riff sounds darker low and brighter high.
exercises.coachLine: Every bar starts on an A. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first lick over A7
exercises.purpose: A written two-bar lick over the shuffle band: down the box from the top A, then home to the A on the D string. The first time the box sounds like a record.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, long-short on the band's triplet, 55 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1: A, C, A, G, E, D, C, D, from the high E string down to the G string. Bar 2: A on the D string, C, G, and the A again, held for two beats.
Swing it the way the drummer does. If the long-short feels odd, say 'tri-pl-et' and play on the 'tri' and the 'et'.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes, so I can check them after the take, and the timing against a shuffle that allows for your own swing.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first twelve bars
exercises.purpose: A whole chorus of the blues in box 1, built the way real players build one: the lick, then the A riff, said again over D7, then a new line over E7 and D7 that comes home. Twelve bars of playing, with the band changing chords under you.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. The band plays A7 for four bars, D7 for two, A7 for two, then E7, D7, A7 and E7.
Bars 1 and 2 are your first lick, and bars 3 and 4 the low and middle A riffs. Bars 5 to 8 are the same four bars again: the lick sounds different over D7 because the chord has moved, not the notes.
Bar 9 starts on E for the E7, bar 10 on D for the D7, bar 11 lands on the middle A, and bar 12 holds E over the E7, which pulls you back to the top.
Shake the last E with a little vibrato if you like. Vibrato isn't graded: the app checks that E was the note and on time, and the shake is yours.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve written bars over the band: I check the notes and the shuffle after the take. The vibrato on the last E isn't graded.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: The box in other keys
steps.goal: Move box 1 to G, C and E and play the lines you already know there, then a whole chorus in a key that changes.
steps.why: The box is a shape, and a shape can start on any fret. The note under your first finger on the low E string names the key: fret 3 is G, fret 5 is A, fret 8 is C, fret 12 is E. Songs are not all in A, and the first time a band calls a blues in G you want your hand to go to fret 3 without thinking. Nothing here is new to the fingers. What is new is finding home somewhere else.
howTo: Find the root on the low E string with your first finger, and the box is under your hand: the same frets as before, counted from there.

Before you play, find the three roots in the new place, as you found the three A's. They are in the same spots in the shape: low E string under the first finger, D string under the third, high E under the first.
Low on the neck the frets are wider and high up they are narrower. Give yourself a slower tempo for the first take in each new place.
steps.payoff: The box is no longer a place at the fifth fret. It goes where the key goes.

exercises.title: The box in G
exercises.purpose: The four-bar box loop from Step 1, two frets lower, over a band in G. Same fingers, same order, a new home.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. First finger on fret 3, third finger on fret 5, fourth on fret 6.

Bar 1 climbs from the low G at fret 3 to C on the G string. Bar 2 goes over the top two strings and holds the high G for two beats. Bar 3 comes down to the G on the D string, fret 5, on beat 3, then F. Bar 4 ends on the low G, held.
Say 'G' on each of the three G's as you pass them.
exercises.coachLine: The same line as Step 1, two frets down. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Three C's in the box at the eighth fret
exercises.purpose: The riff that starts from each root in turn, moved up to C. Low, middle and high C, each opening a bar.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. First finger on fret 8.

Bar 1 starts on the low C (low E string, fret 8). Bar 2 starts on the middle C (D string, fret 10). Bar 3 starts on the high C (high E string, fret 8). Bar 4 comes down and holds the middle C for two beats.
The frets are closer together here than at the fifth fret. Keep one finger per fret and let the hand feel smaller.
exercises.coachLine: The first three bars each start on a C, and the last one lands on a C. I check the notes and the shuffle after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your first lick, at the twelfth fret
exercises.purpose: The two-bar lick from Step 1 in E, up at the twelfth fret where the double dots are. E is the key guitar players call most often.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 55 BPM up to a pass at 90. First finger on fret 12, third finger on fret 14, fourth on fret 15.
Bar 1 comes down from the high E at fret 12 on the top string to the G string. Bar 2 lands on the E on the D string, fret 14, and holds it at the end for two beats.
If the body of the guitar is in the way up here, bring your thumb round toward the bottom of the neck.
exercises.coachLine: The same lick, seven frets up. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Twelve bars in a new key
exercises.purpose: Your first chorus from Step 1, all twelve bars, in G, C or D. The band changes chords in the new key and the same line follows them.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 50 BPM up to a pass at 80. Look at which key came up, put your first finger on its root on the low E string, and play the chorus you know from there: fret 3 for G, fret 8 for C, fret 10 for D.
The form has not changed: four bars on the first chord, two on the second, two back home, then one bar each of the third chord, the second, home, and the third again.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve written bars in a key that changes from day to day. Notes and the shuffle after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: The same notes, a straight feel
steps.goal: Play box 1 in even eighths over a straight rock band, and a twelve-bar chorus of riffs that follow the chords.
steps.why: Half the blues you know is not a shuffle. Rock and roll, and most blues-rock, play the eighth notes even: one-and-two-and, both halves the same length. The notes are the same five and the form is the same twelve bars. Only the feel changes, and a player who has only shuffled will swing a straight groove without meaning to. Playing the same box both ways is how the hand learns the difference.
howTo: Even eighths: 'one-and-two-and', with the 'and' exactly halfway. No long-short. If it starts to lilt, you are shuffling.
Pick down on the beat and up on the 'and'. The riffs here stay on the low strings; rest the side of the picking hand lightly near the bridge so they stay tight.
Listen to the hi-hat. In a straight groove it plays the same even eighths you do.
steps.payoff: You can hear whether a band is shuffling or playing straight, and your eighths follow it.

exercises.title: Box 1, even eighths
exercises.purpose: The four-bar box loop you know, with the band playing straight. The notes are those of Step 1: the only thing to change is how long each eighth is.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Up the box from the low A to D on the G string, over the top and hold the high A, down to the A on the D string, and home to the low A.
Every eighth the same length. Count 'one-and-two-and' out loud for the first take.
exercises.coachLine: Straight eighths now, so the timing bar is tighter than over the shuffle. Notes and evenness after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A straight lick
exercises.purpose: A two-bar lick that runs down the box in even eighths and comes home to A. The kind of line a shuffle would smooth over; here every note is on its own.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Bar 1: A on the top string, then G, E, D, C, and A on the D string, then C and D on the G string. Bar 2: A on the D string for a beat, then G and A, and the A held for two beats.
exercises.coachLine: Notes and even eighths after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A riff on the low strings
exercises.purpose: One bar on the two lowest strings, built on the low A, that loops. Blues-rock rhythm guitar is made of riffs like this one.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 90. One bar, round and round.
A, A, C, A on the low E string (frets 5, 5, 8, 5), then D on the A string, the low A again, and E and D on the A string (frets 7 and 5).
Down-up all the way. The two A's at the start are a down and an up on the same note.
exercises.coachLine: One bar that loops. Notes and even eighths after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Twelve bars of riffs
exercises.purpose: A riff from each chord's root: from A for the A7 bars, from D for the D7 bars, from E for the E7 bar. A whole chorus of rhythm playing, all inside box 1.
howTo: Straight eighths, 60 BPM up to a pass at 85.

Over A7, the riff you just learned. Over D7 it starts on D (A string, fret 5): D, D, E, D, then G on the D string, D, and A and G on the D string. Over E7 it starts on E (A string, fret 7): E, E, G, E, A, E, G, E.
Bar 12 is the ending: E, G, A, G, and E held for two beats. Then the form comes round again.
Each riff starts on its chord's root. If you lose your place, listen for the bass: it is playing the same roots.
exercises.coachLine: Twelve bars over the band. I check the notes and the even eighths after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

steps.title: Chord tones: A7, D7 and E7
steps.goal: Play the arpeggio of each chord of the blues in box 1, and a lick that ends on each chord's third.
steps.why: This is the single biggest step from playing scales to playing changes. A wrong-sounding note is mostly a note that stopped in the wrong place. An arpeggio is the chord one note at a time, so after playing it you know where the chord lives in the box, and a lick that ends on the third says the chord's name out loud.
howTo: A7 is A, C#, E, G. D7 is D, F#, A, C. E7 is E, G#, B, D. The third is the second note of each: C#, F# and G#.
Box 1 has no C#, F# or G#: they sit a fret below or beside its notes. That is why the arpeggios move the hand a little, and why they sound so different from the box.
Aim for the last note first, then get there. Decide on it a beat early.
steps.payoff: The same box suddenly follows the chords, and you can hear the third land.

exercises.title: A on every downbeat
exercises.purpose: Written phrases that land on A at every bar line. The feel of arriving, before it becomes a choice.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 70 BPM up to a pass at 90.
Two beats of A on the D string, then four shuffle eighths that walk away and come back. Land on the next bar line as if it were the point of the whole bar, because it is.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes, and every one of them lands back on A. I check the notes and the shuffle.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The A7 arpeggio, and a lick to C#
exercises.purpose: A7 one note at a time from the low root, then a lick that comes down the box and resolves from C to C#: the blue third to the chord's own third.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: A at fret 5 on the low E (second finger), C# at fret 4 on the A string (first finger), E at 7, G at 5 and A at 7 on the D string, C# at 6 on the G string, E at 5 and G at 8 on the B string. Let the hand move up a fret after the C# on the G string, so the fourth finger reaches fret 8 without a stretch.
Bar 2: G, E, D, C, then C# at fret 6 on the G string for two beats. That half step from C to C# is the sound of the blues resolving.
exercises.coachLine: A written arpeggio and lick: I check each note and the timing after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The D7 arpeggio, and a lick to F#
exercises.purpose: D7 from its root on the A string, then a lick that steps down from G to F#, D7's third. Over the IV chord, that one note is what makes the change audible.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: D at fret 5 on the A string, F# at 4 and A at 7 on the D string, C at 5 and D at 7 on the G string, F# at 7 on the B string, A at 5 and C at 8 on the high E. First finger starts on fret 4 for the F#, and the hand moves up a fret for the top two strings.
Bar 2: A, C, A on the high E, G at fret 8 on the B string, then down a fret to F# and hold it.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes again, checked after the take, with the timing against the shuffle.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: The E7 arpeggio, and a lick to G#
exercises.purpose: E7 from its root at fret 7 on the A string, a step up the neck, then a lick that ends on G#, the third that pulls the form back home to A.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

Bar 1, up: E at fret 7 on the A string, G# at 6 and B at 9 on the D string, D at 7 and E at 9 on the G string, G# at 9 on the B string, B at 7 and D at 10 on the high E. First finger on fret 6, then up a fret for the top two strings.
Bar 2: B, D, B on the high E, A at 10 on the B string, then down a fret to G# and hold it. It's the D7 lick moved up a tone.
exercises.coachLine: Written notes, checked after the take, and the timing against the band's shuffle.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Your turn: land on a chord tone
exercises.purpose: Your choice now. Over A7, D7, E7 and A7, make a little phrase in each bar that lands on beat 1 of the next on one of that chord's notes. Anything goes in between.
howTo: Shuffle, 70 to 90 BPM, four bars that loop.
Land on A, C#, E or G over A7; D, F#, A or C over D7; E, G#, B or D over E7. The written line is one way it could go, not a target.
Your turn, and not checked yet: the app can't judge notes you choose, so you tick it off yourself.
exercises.coachLine: Not checked yet: landings are yours to judge for now. Record it and listen to beat 1 of each bar.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

selfCheck: On beat 1 of every bar, was your note one of that chord's four?
Did you decide on the landing note before you got there?

steps.difficultyException: The note rate sits a little under Step 1, whose twelve-bar chorus runs over three chords; the new demand here is three notes outside the box, C#, F# and G#, and a hand that moves a fret to reach them, which the rate does not count.

steps.title: Call and response
steps.goal: Hear a phrase, answer it, and leave space: the conversation that blues is built on.
steps.why: Blues is a conversation, and most beginners only ever talk. Answering a phrase teaches you to phrase in lengths a listener can follow, and it forces you to stop playing. It does more for how you sound, per minute, than any scale you can learn.
howTo: Listen to the whole call before you play. Don't start your answer until it has finished.
Keep your answer about as long as the call. Two bars of question deserves two bars of answer.
Silence is a note. A bar with nothing in it is a decision, and a good one.
steps.payoff: You can trade two-bar phrases with the app and it sounds like a conversation.

exercises.title: Echo
exercises.purpose: The app plays a two-bar phrase; you play it back, note for note. Exercising the ear is what this is for.
howTo: Straight eighths and quarters, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. Bars 1 and 2 are the call, bars 3 and 4 are yours.
Try not to look at the tab. Sing the phrase back before you play it, once, if you can.
exercises.coachLine: After the take I can say if the echo had the right notes and steady time. It's fine to take a few tries.
exercises.feedbackNote: The app has to play the call: the synth voice can do that, and the Exercise format carries it as a guide part, but nothing wires that up yet, so the call is in the tab for now.

exercises.title: One call, four answers
exercises.purpose: The same call four times, and four written answers to it. Each ends somewhere else: on the root, the fifth, the flat seven and the high blue third. Hear what an ending does.
howTo: Straight eighths and quarters, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80. Sixteen bars: call, answer, call, answer.
Answer 1 ends on A (finished). Answer 2 ends on E (open). Answer 3 ends on G (it wants to go on). Answer 4 climbs to the high C (it hangs in the air).
Let each last note ring through its two beats, then stop.
exercises.coachLine: Four written answers: I check the notes and the time after the take. Which ending you like best is yours.
exercises.feedbackNote: The calls are a guide part the app does not play yet, so they are in the tab for now.

exercises.title: Two bars on, two bars off
exercises.purpose: Over the band, a written phrase for two bars, then two bars of nothing, then another phrase. Most players find the stopping much harder than the playing.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, 70 BPM up to a pass at 90. Eight bars: phrase, rest, phrase, rest.
Count the two silent bars out loud if you have to. Your hands come off the strings, and the band plays on.
exercises.coachLine: Written phrases, checked for notes and time. A note in the empty bars shows up as an extra note, so leave them empty.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: Free trade
exercises.purpose: The app calls, you answer however you like. This is the one that sounds most like playing blues with someone. Ungraded, because a good answer isn't something the app can judge.
howTo: Straight time, 60 to 80 BPM. The call is bars 1 and 2, your answer bars 3 and 4.
Answer with whatever comes. Try once with very few notes and once with a lot, and hear which you like better.
exercises.coachLine: No marks on this one. Enjoy it, and listen back if you recorded.

steps.difficultyException: The note rate falls because half of these bars are silence; listening and leaving space is the new demand, which is not a rate.

steps.title: Landing on the third, in new keys
steps.goal: Play the arpeggio and its lick to the third in G and C, then a twelve-bar chorus whose phrases stop on each chord's third.
steps.why: You have met the two ideas that matter most at this Level: the box moves with the key, and a phrase sounds right when it stops on a note of the chord. This Step puts them together before anything new arrives. The third is the note that says whether a chord is major, so a phrase that stops on it tells the listener which chord the band is on, with no band needed.
howTo: The third of the home chord sits one fret above the minor pentatonic's own third: in A, C# is one fret above C. In every key it is the same move, one fret up on the same string.

The thirds in A: C# over A7 (G string, fret 6), F# over D7 (D string, fret 4), G# over E7 (D string, fret 6). The F# is a fret below the box, so the first finger reaches back for it. So is the B over E7 (G string, fret 4).
Hold each landing note for its full two beats. The rest of the phrase is the way there.
steps.payoff: A chorus with no band would still tell a listener where the changes are.

exercises.title: G7, and a lick to B
exercises.purpose: The arpeggio and lick you learned over A7, two frets lower. G7 is G, B, D, F, and the lick resolves from B flat to B.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bar 1, up: G at fret 3 on the low E, B at fret 2 on the A string, D at 5, F at 3 and G at 5 on the D string, B at 4 on the G string, D at 3 and F at 6 on the B string.
Bar 2: F, D, C, B flat, then B at fret 4 on the G string for two beats.
exercises.coachLine: The A7 line moved to G. I check each note and the timing after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: C7, and a lick to E
exercises.purpose: The same arpeggio and lick at the eighth fret. C7 is C, E, G, B flat, and the lick resolves from E flat to E.
howTo: Shuffle eighths, then a half note, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bar 1, up: C at fret 8 on the low E, E at fret 7 on the A string, G at 10, B flat at 8 and C at 10 on the D string, E at 9 on the G string, G at 8 and B flat at 11 on the B string.
Bar 2: B flat, G, F, E flat, then E at fret 9 on the G string for two beats.
exercises.coachLine: The same line in C. I check each note and the timing after the take.

notes: With a microphone and speakers the band reaches the same input as you. Direct input or headphones are the honest way to grade this; without them it is untested.

exercises.title: A chorus that lands
exercises.purpose: Twelve bars in A where the phrases over A7 stop on C#, the phrases over D7 stop on F#, and the phrase over E7 stops on G#. Short phrases, long landings, and the root in between.
howTo: Shuffle eighths and half notes, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.
Bars 1 to 4, over A7: a phrase to C# (G string, fret 6), the A held, a second phrase to C#, and a bar that sits on A.

steps.title: The blues scale and the blue notes
steps.goal: Add the flat five as a note to pass through, and hear the third move from C to C#.
steps.why: Two notes turn a scale into the blues. The flat five, Eb in A, sounds wrong on its own and wonderful on its way somewhere else. The blue third, C rubbing against the chord's C#, is the tension the whole style runs on. You've been playing the C already; now you'll hear what it's doing.
howTo: The A blues scale is A, C, D, Eb, E, G. Eb lives at fret 6 on the A string and fret 8 on the G string in this box.
Don't park on the Eb. Walk through it on your way to D or E.
To resolve the blue third, hammer from C to C# with your first and second fingers on the G string.
steps.payoff: One extra note, and suddenly the lick sounds like the blues rather than a rock scale.

exercises.title: A blues scale, box 1
exercises.purpose: The box with its one new note, so you can find the Eb without thinking.
howTo: Straight eighths, two to a click, 60 BPM up to a pass at 80.

exercises.coachLine: Right notes and even eighths after the take, the same as before.

exercises.title: Passing, not parking
exercises.purpose: A lick with the flat five exactly where it belongs: on the way from D to E, and back from E to D.

Bar 1: D, Eb on the G string, E and G on the B string, back to E, then Eb, D and C on the G string. Bar 2: A on the D string, C, A, then the G held for two beats. The Eb never lands.
exercises.coachLine: The Eb goes by quickly. I check the notes and the time after the take; how it sounds is what you're listening for.

exercises.title: From C to C#

steps.title: Following the 12-bar
steps.goal: Know where you are in the form without counting bars, and hear the turnaround coming.
steps.why: Losing your place is the number one bedroom problem. The form is twelve bars: four of A7, two of D7, two of A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Once it's in your ear you stop counting and start anticipating, and that's when solos start to have a shape. Playing the bass line is the fastest way there: you can't get lost when you're the one playing it.
howTo: Count the form as 4 + 4 + 4, as the Jam timeline does. Each four is a sentence.
Listen for the bar 9 change to E7. It's the moment the form really moves.
Bars 11 and 12 are the turnaround: they exist only to bring you back to the top.
steps.payoff: You hear the changes coming, and you can play a whole written chorus that brings the form home.

steps.title: The quick change
steps.goal: Follow the twelve-bar form when it goes to the D7 in bar 2, with roots, a boogie line and a written chorus.
steps.why: Many blues songs do not sit on the first chord for four bars. They go to the second chord in bar 2 and come straight back: the quick change. Nothing else in the form moves. A player who has learned the form by counting gets caught by it every time; a player who listens hears it coming. It is the same twelve bars with one bar different, which makes it a good test of whether you know the form or only its length.
howTo: The form: A7, D7, A7, A7, then D7, D7, A7, A7, then E7, D7, A7, E7. Only bar 2 is new.
Before you play, listen to the band once through and point at bar 2 when the chord moves.
Everything you play here uses notes and shapes you already know: the roots and the boogie line from the last Step, and the thirds from the Beginner Level. What changes is when.
steps.payoff: When a band goes to the IV chord in bar 2, you are already there.

steps.title: Bends that land
steps.goal: Bend a note up to an exact pitch, on time, and come back down from it.
steps.why: A bend is the guitar's voice, and it's only expressive when it arrives. A bend that stops short sounds like a mistake in a way a wrong note often doesn't. The way to learn it is simple, and it's old: play the note you want, then bend up to it and compare.
howTo: Bend with three fingers on the string, ring finger on the note. Push from the wrist, as if turning a door handle, rather than from the fingers alone.
Play the target first. Then bend until there's no wobble left between what you hear and what you remember.
The app times your bends and doesn't measure how far they go, so your ear judges the pitch on every one of these. Keep your strings fresh: old strings make this much harder.
steps.payoff: A bent note that sits on the band's chord tone and arrives on the beat.

steps.title: Question and answer phrases
steps.goal: Play phrases that ask and phrases that resolve, and build a twelve-bar chorus from them.
steps.why: A phrase that ends on the root sounds finished. A phrase that ends anywhere else sounds like a question. Knowing that gives you the shape of almost every blues vocal ever sung: say it, say it again, then answer it. It's the point where you stop stringing licks together and start saying something.
howTo: A question often ends on G or C, and an answer ends on A. Start both the same way and only change the ending: the listener hears the relationship.
Blues lyric form is A, A, B: the same line twice, then the reply. Use that form on the guitar.
Over D7, the same line sounds different, which is why repeating it doesn't get boring.
steps.payoff: A twelve-bar chorus that has a beginning, a middle and an end, and uses very few notes.

steps.title: The minor blues
steps.goal: Play the arpeggios of Am7 and Dm7, find the F and the G# that a minor blues needs, and play a written chorus over the minor form.
steps.why: A minor blues has the same twelve bars with minor chords on the first two: Am7 and Dm7, and still E7 for the turn. The good news is that the box fits the first chord perfectly, since Am7 is four of its five notes. The catch is the Dm7: its third is F, and there is no F in the box. Play the box's E over a Dm7 for long and it sounds unsure. One new note, F on the B string, fixes it, and G# over the E7 does the rest.
howTo: Am7 is A, C, E, G: all in box 1. Dm7 is D, F, A, C: F is at fret 6 on the B string, one fret above the box's E, and at fret 8 on the A string. E7 is E, G#, B, D, as before.
Over Dm7, play F where you would have played E. Over Am7, go back to E. It is a one-fret move up on one string, like C to C#. This time the higher note is the minor one.
A minor blues is usually slower and sadder. Leave the long notes long.
steps.payoff: A slow minor chorus where the F arrives with the Dm7 and the G# with the E7.

Bar 3, Dm7 up: D and F on the A string (frets 5 and 8), A on the D string (7), C and D on the G string (5 and 7), F on the B string (6), A and C on the top string (5 and 8). Bar 4: F, D, C, D, and F held.

steps.title: Connecting box 1 and box 2
steps.goal: Move between the first two pentatonic boxes through shared notes, without the seam showing.
steps.why: One box keeps you in a cage. The way out isn't to learn all five at once: it's to find one door. Box 2 uses the same five notes, a little higher, and the G string gives you a slide from one box into the other. That's enough to change how your solos sound, because a higher note on the same scale is a whole new emotion in the phrase.
howTo: Box 2 starts at fret 7 or 8: on the G string it is frets 7 and 9, on the B string frets 8 and 10.
The door is a slide on the G string from D at fret 7 up to E at fret 9. Slide with your third finger and you land in position in box 2.
Box 1 and box 2 are the same notes. A on the D string, fret 7, is the same in both, and you've already found it.
steps.payoff: Your lick climbs out of the box, reaches a new high note, and comes home again.

exercises.title: Box 2, up and down
exercises.purpose: The new shape on its own: the same notes in a new layout.

exercises.title: The door: slide up, come home

steps.title: Boxes 3 and 4: up to the twelfth fret
steps.goal: Play the next two pentatonic boxes, find the second door between box 2 and box 3, and play one line from the fifth fret to the twelfth.
steps.why: Two boxes gave you one door. Two more take you to the twelfth fret, where the neck starts again an octave up, and after that there is only one shape left to learn. The reason to go there is the sound: the same notes further up the neck sit on thicker strings and sound fuller, and the top of box 3 reaches notes box 1 does not have. The second door is a slide on the top string from D at fret 10 to E at fret 12, with the third finger. It puts your hand in box 3.

steps.title: Major and minor together
steps.goal: Play the sweet major pentatonic over the A7 chord and go back to the minor one when the D7 arrives, and hear why.
steps.why: The minor pentatonic over a blues is the sound you already have: tough, a little sour. The players people call sweet mix in the major pentatonic over the first chord, because its C# is the third of A7. Then the D7 arrives, C# clashes with it, and C natural, the minor note, is suddenly the right one. Changing one note with the chord is the first step from playing a scale to playing the changes.
howTo: A major pentatonic is A, B, C#, E, F#. At the fifth fret it sits a fret lower than box 1: the first finger moves back to fret 4 on the A, D and G strings.
Over A7, aim for C# (G string, fret 6). Over D7, aim for C (G string, fret 5). One fret apart, and each is a note of its own chord.
The high position at fret 10, with the first finger on A on the B string, is where a lot of the sweetest blues phrases live. Nothing in it needs a stretch.
steps.payoff: A phrase that smiles over the A7 and frowns over the D7, and a high lick at the tenth fret with the sixth in it.

steps.title: Sixths
steps.goal: Play two-note sixths on the G and top strings over A7, D7 and E7, through the whole form and at the end of a lick.
steps.why: A sixth is two notes six scale steps apart. On the guitar here that means two notes of the chord with a string between them, and it is the sound of a great many blues intros, fills and endings. One small shape gives you A7; move the lower note down a fret and it is D7; move the whole shape up two frets from there and it is E7. That is the whole form in three shapes that sit within three frets of each other, which makes sixths the easiest way to play the changes with more than one note.
howTo: A7: C# on the G string (fret 6) with A on the top string (fret 5). D7: C on the G string (fret 5) with A on the top string (fret 5). E7: D on the G string (fret 7) with B on the top string (fret 7).

The B string between them must not ring. Either pick the G string and pluck the top string with your middle finger, or let the fretting finger on the G string lean on the B string and strum through all three.
Up the neck, the A7 sixths walk: frets 6 and 5, then 7 and 7, then 9 and 9. The first is slanted, the next two are straight across.
steps.payoff: The twelve bars played in sixths, and a lick that ends on one.

steps.title: Guide tones through the changes
steps.goal: Hear and play the thirds and sevenths that make each chord what it is, and move between them by half steps.
steps.why: If you only play two notes per chord, these are the two. The third and seventh of a dominant chord tell the ear exactly what's happening, and from one chord to the next they barely move: G falls a half step to F#, C# falls to C. Play that, and the changes appear in a single line with no band at all. It's the moment theory turns into something you can hear.
howTo: A7's guide tones are C# and G. D7's are F# and C. E7's are G# and D.
G to F# (A7 to D7) and C# to C (A7 to D7) are half steps. E7's G# is the odd one out: go up a tone from F# on the B string.

steps.payoff: A single slow line that spells the whole twelve-bar form without any other notes.

steps.title: Slow blues
steps.goal: Play a full written chorus at a slow tempo, where every note you play is on display.

howTo: Feel the triplets under the beat: each beat has three pulses, and the drummer plays them on the hat.
Play less than you think. Let a held note ring through a chord change if it still fits, and hear how it changes.
Use vibrato only once a note has landed, not to find it.
steps.payoff: Twelve slow bars that sound like a blues player, with the space to prove it.
